p: The Monday after April drill, Kit printed her letter of intent with her own sentence at the bottom, I want to fly, and deleted the old one. Graham had left a note on the coffee maker that said garage. The tarp was off the crib, and clipped to its top rail were seven index cards, the seven Physical Science questions she'd missed on his practice test, question on the front, answer on the back. That was his answer to her note. When he came home he told her it wasn't a question. He wasn't asking her for anything with it. He'd just gotten tired of it waiting in the dark for after, and it could wait out there with them. She asked which grit he started with. They sanded on study nights from then on, with the cards on the rail.

At Vern's table that Tuesday he looked at the family day picture a long time. He'd told her that was the best seat on the airplane, he said, and the Lieutenant, and Patrice for fifty years. Then he told her what the back seat had cost him, and told her not to let her own story do the same. Kit said hers had been an inspection. His had been a seat, he said, and they were both real, which was why they worked so well. He printed rationalize on an envelope and put it in his shirt pocket.

At the plant, Gene's new feed chart ran flow down the side, and Kit caught her hand going to where the old number used to sit, and read the labels first. Graham brought maple blocks home from his lab and built piles on the kitchen table, and she learned to count only blocks that share a face, plus the ones she couldn't see that had to be there, because nothing floats.

On the May drill she asked Fisk, alone and as a favor, to time her at lunch. Then Colonel Merritt asked her why a second time. Kit said she wanted to fly, for herself, since a family day when she was seven, and that she'd missed the pilot score in 2019 and told everybody she'd stayed for an inspection. Merritt asked her the number. Nineteen, ma'am, Kit said.

When Kit called it a waiver, Merritt corrected her once. It's an exception to policy, and the unit sponsors it, and that's her. Her name on it was necessary and not enough, she said. The yes comes from above the wing, and she'd endorse it only if Kit's number let her. She told Kit about Corbin, the airman she'd sent on heart, and asked what Kit wanted from her. Your name on the exception to policy, ma'am, if the number earns it, Kit said. I'll bring you the number. On Sunday Corbin told Kit the colonel asks him first, every time, and he lets her because she asks.

The night before her second practice test Kit stopped before midnight and went to bed. Table Reading came back thirty eight of forty, and Block Counting twenty seven of thirty. That night in the garage Graham put his hand over hers on the sanding block and let her steer, and nobody said July.
The test administrator. Pearson's staff member at the test center in Kansas City where Kit sits the test. She checks IDs against the confirmation and hands out the locker keys.

The launch board in the shop had one line on it for the weekend, at twenty to three on Friday, May 14. Two two eight, Saturday, wheels up at 0730. A training sortie the full timers had set up off the drill schedule, because a new copilot needed the hours. Beside it, in Boyd's grease pencil, out of habit or not, DARROW.
Kit had slept four hours off a Thursday night at the plant. At noon Boyd had texted her three lines, which for Boyd was a letter.
A text from Boyd. Sat sortie is 228. You're in KC. Come see me.

His door was open. He was reading a forms binder that wasn't hers and didn't look up. You're in Kansas City at eight tomorrow. She flies at seven thirty. Somebody launches her. He turned a page. Your jet, Darrow. You pick who.

Out his window Fisk was at the nose of two two eight with the intake covers stacked at his feet, counting them the way she'd taught him, one hand on each. He was on orders for the weekend. On Wednesday he'd told her, without being asked, that he'd gotten Friday night off from the warehouse too. His lead owed him one, he said, for all the Fridays.
In April, by the medevac pad, Fisk had asked her. Who's on her then? She hadn't answered him.
I'll say it once more, Sergeant, in the order it comes, and then I'll quit talking about the order for good.

The current Pearson page lists twelve subtests, and you sit them in one run. Verbal Analogies, 25 questions in 8 minutes. Arithmetic Reasoning, 25 in 29. Word Knowledge, 25 in 5. Math Knowledge, 25 in 22. Reading Comprehension, 25 in 24. Situational Judgment, 16 in 35. Then the one scheduled break, fifteen minutes. After it, the Self Description Inventory, 240 statements in 45 minutes, not graded. Then Physical Science, 20 in 10. Table Reading, 40 in 7. Instrument Comprehension, 25 in 5. Block Counting, 30 in 5. Aviation Information, 20 in 8, and you're done.

Add up the clocks and it's three hours and twenty three minutes. The break makes it three thirty eight. Check in and the tutorial screens stretch it to about five, which is what Pearson tells you to plan on. The 2015 pamphlet had different numbers for three of those blocks, 38 minutes on reading, 50 judgment picks, four and a half minutes on blocks. So read your own confirmation, and if it disagrees with me, believe it and not me. I've been wrong about schedules before. I once told a whole crew the chow hall at Lajes opened at five. It opened at six. They remembered that one a long time.
How the exam asks it. Know the order and every clock before you walk in, so nothing on the screen is news.

You can't book without a voucher, from a recruiter or a base test control officer, and the test costs you nothing. Your confirmation email names the center, the time and what to bring for ID. Read it the night before, all the way to the bottom, and put the ID in your coat. A test center can't seat you on a good attitude.

Eat breakfast. Five hours is a long time on coffee, and the break doesn't come until somewhere past the two hour mark. Get there early enough to park without hurrying. Everything you carry goes into a locker, so bring nothing you'd miss for five hours, and nothing you'd want to read once the doors close. That includes your notes. If it isn't in your head by the parking lot, it won't be in your head at question nine.

In the truck, do five analogies out loud as sentences, and stop there. A chock keeps a wheel from moving. Whatever you say in that seat, say it in a sentence, so the first block isn't the first time your head's been asked to work today. No new words. No new math. I flew a checkride in 1976 with a pilot who studied the emergency procedures in the crew bus the whole way out. He got one of them backward an hour later, the one he'd read last.
How the exam asks it. ID in your coat the night before. Eat. Five spoken analogies in the truck, and then nothing new.
Here's the pace on each of the first six, and what I'd have you do on it.

Verbal Analogies, nineteen seconds or so a question. Turn the first pair into a sentence and try every choice in it. Whichever one you could say to a stranger at the Riverside without him looking at you funny, that's yours. Don't pick a pair for being about airplanes. Arithmetic Reasoning gives you about seventy seconds, and it comes right after the fastest thinking of the day, so read the first problem twice. Your eyes are still going analogy speed. Find out what they want, gallons or minutes or dollars, before you write a number down.

Word Knowledge, twelve seconds a word, and that's not long. Know it or guess it, and go. Look for the pieces, and check whether the word praises or knocks before you pick. Math Knowledge, about fifty three. Quick ones buy time for geometry. Got an x? Put it back where it came from. If the two sides don't match, you slipped, and I'd bet my ring it was a minus sign. On a long one with clean numbers in the choices, try the choices.

Reading Comprehension, twenty four minutes for twenty five questions on the current page. That's a minute each with the reading thrown in, and it's not much of a minute. I'd read a passage one time through for the bones of it. Then go hunting for the line each question's about, and put a finger on it like you're holding your place in a hymnal. Situational Judgment is thirty five minutes. Sixteen problems on the screen is two minutes and change for each. Twenty five would be a minute twenty four. Count them when the block opens, Sergeant, and pick your halfway from that.
How the exam asks it. Read the first word problem twice, because it comes right after the fastest block of the morning.

I'll give you the judgment key one last time, the three parts we haven't leaned on since March. The first is leadership. The test wants the officer who takes charge of what's theirs and deals with a people problem directly, in private, at the lowest level that can fix it, and goes up the chain when that try fails. It wants expectations set out loud. And it wants the credit going to the people who did the work.

Handing off a job is where leadership shows. A good handover gives the person the work and the decisions that come with it, tells everybody who's in charge, and names someone in the chain they can call that isn't you. Then you leave. Checking every hour isn't a handover. Neither is sending somebody to watch them behind their back. A handover with your hand still on it is usually the middle answer on the test, right in spirit and wrong in grip.

In 1982 I handed my first student navigator the chart over Iowa and sat on my hands for three hours. He put us eleven miles left of course and found it himself. If I'd taken the pencil, he'd have learned that I take the pencil. The test calls that delegation. My instructor in 1974 called it shutting up, and he was the better teacher.
How the exam asks it. Most effective hands over the job and the authority together. A handover you keep checking on is the partial.

The second part is resource management, which is a long name for knowing what you've got and not wasting it. People's hours, people's rest, the budget, the one truck that runs. When two jobs both want Thursday, the test likes the officer who tells their boss early, lays out both, and asks which comes first. It doesn't like the one who quietly lets a deadline slip, and it doesn't like the one who works everybody all night so nobody has to have the conversation.

Two more patterns. If only one person in your section can do a task, the right move is to get a second person trained now, on the schedule, while the first one is still around to teach. Hoping the replacement shows up knowing it is how a section gets stuck. And when you're cutting something, cut it with the people who know where the money really goes, and tell your boss what the cut will cost before it costs it.

People are on that list too, and their rest is part of the budget. A tired crew is a resource you've already spent. The key leans toward the plan that gets the work done and looks after the people doing it, and away from the one that buys today with next week.
How the exam asks it. Two tasks, one deadline: tell your boss now and ask which first. A quiet slip or an all nighter ranks low.

The third is mentoring, and it's the one officers get wrong by being good at things. When somebody you supervise does a job their own way, slower than yours and inside the rules, let them finish. Ask them afterward, in private, how they decided on it, and offer yours as one more way. Taking it out of their hands teaches them to wait for you.

When a capable airman won't step up, give them a piece they can win. One part of the brief, not the whole exercise, with you there to help them get ready and a talk afterward about how it went. Throwing them in front of the whole squadron is a test of nerve, not a lesson. Telling them they'll never make rank unless they speak up is a threat, and the test usually ranks threats near the bottom.

Coaching is mostly questions. Counseling is private. Feedback has a time on it, soon. I had a navigator named Doug, in 1984, who didn't trust his own fixes. For a month I asked him where we were and made him tell me before I'd look. By summer he quit asking me to check. That's the whole job, and the hard part is the asking.
How the exam asks it. Let them finish their way if it's inside the rules, then talk in private. Taking over, or correcting in public, ranks low.

The break comes after Situational Judgment, and it's fifteen minutes on the current page. Use it on your body. Eat something with salt in it. Drink water. Use the restroom whether you think you need it or not. Stand up and walk the length of the lobby twice. Then sit back down before they come for you.

Don't replay the first half. You can't change one answer from the lobby, and the inventory and five more blocks, three of them speed blocks, are still ahead of you. If you catch yourself working an arithmetic problem from an hour ago, look out a window at something far away. A parked truck will do. Your eyes have been eighteen inches from a screen all morning, and the next three clocks are all eyes.
On a long track I'd eat half a sandwich at the halfway point whether I wanted it or not. The boom operators thought it was funny. I never once lost a fix after the sandwich.
How the exam asks it. Spend the break on your body, not on the first half.

The Self Description Inventory is next: 240 statements in 45 minutes, about eleven seconds each, on a five point agree scale. It isn't graded, and nothing you mark there counts toward a composite. It's there to help match people to jobs, which is why you answer it as yourself.

There are no right answers. The only way to do it badly is to answer as somebody else, the officer you think they're hoping for. Answer each one with your first honest mark and move to the next. Quick and consistent, because it's the same you on statement two hundred as on statement two. Don't go hunting for what each one is for. Don't save any for later. Pearson's page says each question must be answered to receive results, so every one gets a mark.

It's also a long stretch where nothing's scored, sitting between two clocks that are. Keep your pace easy, keep your back straight, and save your eyes. If you finish early, close them for a minute. The speed blocks come in fast after this, and you'll want everything you didn't spend.
How the exam asks it. No right answers. First honest mark on every statement, and keep your eyes for what comes after.

Physical Science is twenty questions in ten minutes, thirty seconds each. Most are recall, so know it or guess, and spend your seconds on the few with one step of math. Check the units before you multiply anything.

Then the three speed blocks, back to back, with a new set of eyes for each. Table Reading, forty in seven, about ten and a half seconds a question. Column, then row, then the cell, then the choices. Instrument Comprehension, twenty five in five, about twelve seconds. Compass first, because it it's the quickest cue to read, then bank, then pitch, and cross off the moment a cue misses. Block Counting, thirty in five, about ten seconds. Learn each pile on its first question, count in the same order every time, and remember the blocks you can't see are holding up the ones you can.

Aviation Information comes last, twenty in eight, twenty four seconds each. It's the end of a long day and it feeds the Pilot composite, so don't let it go soft on you. Know it or guess, keep moving, and finish with something marked on every question. I've watched people sit back after Block Counting like the day was over. It's the last eight minutes, and they count.
How the exam asks it. Compass first on the dials. The same order on the blocks. Don't let the last eight minutes go soft.

One of them will. It might be the dials, or a reading passage that won't hold still, or a pile that looks like somebody dropped it. Here's what you do. Mark your best guess on the question in front of you. Take one breath, all the way out. Then go back to your order, the one you practiced, and do the next question as if it were the first.

A bad block doesn't decide the morning. The composites mix several subtests, so one slow block gets diluted by the others. Your best score on each composite counts across your tries, and a Form T score doesn't expire. The only way a bad block costs you twice is if you carry it into the next one. Each clock starts fresh when it starts. Let it.

In 1979, over Newfoundland, I lost the stars for forty minutes in high cloud and had to dead reckon on a wind I didn't trust. When they came back I was nine miles off and furious with myself. My aircraft commander said, Pruett, where are we now? Not where were we. Now. I've used that question on every bad day since, including a few that had nothing to do with airplanes.
How the exam asks it. Guess on the one in front of you, breathe once, and start the next question clean.
The last minute of every block.

Every block ends the same way. You've got a minute left and questions you haven't reached. Scoring is built from the number you get right, and nothing comes off for a wrong answer, so a blank and a wrong answer cost you the same. Pearson wants every one answered anyway.

So with about a minute left, look at what's open. If you can work one more honestly, do it. With twenty seconds left, stop working and mark every open question, on purpose, before the clock does it for you. Pick one letter and use it all the way down if you like. A guess you chose is better than a question the clock took.

In 2019 Kit ran out on the dials with nine left. I didn't know her then, but I know what that feels like, a screen ending while you're still reading. Watch the clock at halfway and again at the last minute, and the clock never surprises you.
How the exam asks it. No penalty for a wrong answer. At twenty seconds, mark everything that's still open.

Five setups carry most of Arithmetic Reasoning, and you know all five. Amount is rate times time: have two, get the third. Say the crew bus goes 18 miles at 36 miles an hour. Eighteen over thirty six is half an hour. A ratio is a fraction you can cross multiply. If 2 of every 5 bolts in a bin are steel and the bin holds 45, it's 18 steel and 27 not, and they'll ask for whichever one you didn't find.

Percent change goes over the number you started with. Fifty sorties in March and sixty in April is ten over fifty, up 20 percent. The trap is ten over sixty, about 17, which is the percent you'd get going back down. Two people working together, add their rates, not their times. And an average is a total over a count, so to find a missing score, find the total you need and take away what you've got.

Then the habits. Units next to every number. A rough guess before you work it, so a wrong answer looks wrong. Check the answer against the question they asked, because the number you found on the way is usually sitting in the choices too. I've got a dispatcher's habit of saying the units out loud, pounds, hours, gallons, and Patrice says I do it in my sleep. I'd rather be teased than short of fuel.
How the exam asks it. Set it up with units, guess the size, then check you answered what they asked.

Equations. Get the letter by itself. Whatever you do to the left, do to the right. A loadmaster at Dover showed me that with two sandbags and a broom handle in 1975, and I've forgotten his name and never the broom handle. Watch the minus signs. They're small and they wander. Say it's 3(x plus 2) equals x plus 14. Multiply out the left and it's 3x plus 6. Take x away from both, then 6 from both. Two x is 8. X is 4. Then you put the 4 back in, because I said so. Three times six, 18. Four and fourteen, 18. That one's done.

Right triangles. There are a few whole number families on this test the way there are a few families in Tolliver, the 3, 4, 5s and the 5, 12, 13s, and they show up doubled at reunions. Long side 10, short side 6? That's the 3, 4, 5s, twice. Missing side, 8. If you don't see the family, square the two short ones, add, and take the root of that. Circles. Pi r squared inside, 2 pi r around. Half the time they hand you the distance around and want the area. So you dig the radius out first. Six pi around, radius 3, area 9 pi. Patrice says I explain circles like a man who lost an argument to one.

Exponents. Same base, multiplying? You add the little numbers. Power of a power, multiply them. Two squared times two cubed, two to the fifth, 32. The answer two to the sixth will be sitting in the choices with its hand up. Binomials, every term times every term, and the two inside numbers make the middle. (x plus 5)(x minus 2) is x squared, then 5x and minus 2x for 3x, then minus 10. I did algebra on the back of fuel logs for twenty years, and nobody checked it but me, which is why I checked it.
How the exam asks it. Plug your answer back in. Find the radius before you use a circle. Same base, add the exponents.

Scores post in two to three business days on the current Pearson page. You look them up yourself on the AFOQT score page linked from Pearson's site, with your Social Security number, last name and test center number. If they're not there, call your recruiter or test control officer. They come back as composite percentiles, one to ninety nine: Pilot, Combat Systems Officer, Air Battle Manager, Academic Aptitude, Verbal and Quantitative, with Situational Judgment reported on its own. Every commission needs Verbal 15 and Quantitative 10. A rated job needs 25 on its own composite.

If a number comes up short, you can sit it again, at least 90 days after the last time, and a third try takes a waiver. Your best score on each composite stands, so a second try can only raise a number. Form T scores don't expire. If you're headed for a pilot board, the Pilot composite goes into your PCSM score along with the TBAS, which is a separate computer test, and your logged flying hours. Your unit's posting may set a PCSM minimum of its own, so read it again, line by line, and book the TBAS if it asks.
That's the test, Sergeant. You've had all of it now. I said I'd quit talking about the order, and I will.
How the exam asks it. Two to three business days. Best composite counts. Ninety days between tries. Read your posting for a PCSM floor.
She went out to the nose. The ramp was warm for once, and somebody's radio on the next jet was playing a ball game nobody on it was listening to.
Fisk straightened up from the covers. Who's launching her tomorrow, Sergeant? Sergeant Kemp's free. I heard him say.

Two two eight sat there between them, sixty five years old, the forms binder in its slot by the crew door. Kit had launched her more times than she could count. On the morning of the paper test in 2019 Boyd had launched her, and Kit had told herself all the way to the test office that it didn't matter who.
The launch is Kit's to give away. How does she hand two two eight to Fisk?
A. Walk her with him and hand him the forms for Saturday.
B. Have Kemp look over his shoulder in the morning, and not mention it to him.
C. Plan to come in at four herself and do the walkaround before she drives.
D. Give him the jet with two pages of notes, and ask him to text her each step.

You asked me in April who's on her. You are. Saturday first. Fisk didn't say anything. She walked her with him nose to tail, the way Boyd had walked her once, and stopped at the crew door and handed him the binder. Boyd's your backup. Not me. I'll be in a room with no phone. He held the binder against his vest with both arms. What if they call a delay? Then it's your call and Boyd's. He nodded once and went to put the covers away, and she saw him touch each one again on the way.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Leadership and Mentoring. You gave him the work and the decisions with it, said so plainly, and named his backup in the chain, which isn't you. Then you got out of the way. The key leans hard toward a handover like that: clear, complete and trusted. Then you walked away from it, which is the part most people skip.

Graham had the truck running in the driveway at ten after five, and Orchard Street was still dark. A thermos between them. A milk crate on the floor at her feet with ninety six lab reports in it and a red pen clipped to the visor. It was Fisk on the ramp this morning. She'd lain awake a while on that and then slept, which surprised her.
At six her phone went off on the dash. Fisk. She put him on speaker. Behind him a power cart was running, and somebody was yelling about a ladder.

I pulled the order up off the Pearson page Wednesday on my break. Verbal Analogies, twenty five in eight. Arithmetic Reasoning, twenty five in twenty nine. Word Knowledge, twenty five in five. Math Knowledge, twenty five in twenty two. Reading Comprehension, twenty five in twenty four. Situational Judgment, sixteen in thirty five. Then fifteen minutes.
Graham, driving, nodded at the road as if Fisk could see him. She heard paper move on the other end. He'd written it out.

Then the inventory, two forty in forty five. Physical Science, twenty in ten. Table Reading, forty in seven. Instrument Comprehension, twenty five in five. Block Counting, thirty in five. Aviation Information, twenty in eight. That's all of them. He took a breath. You want me to call you if anything comes up on her?
He's offered to keep her posted on the jet. What does Kit tell him?
A. Tell him to call her the second anything looks wrong, test or no test.
B. Ask him to text her once two two eight is off the ground, so she'll know.
C. Tell him she's his today and to call Boyd if anything comes up.
D. Have him read her the forms over the phone before she goes in.
She's yours today, Fisk. Anything comes up, you call Boyd. There was a little pause, just the power cart. Copy, Sergeant. Then, quieter, Go get it. He hung up first. He'd never done that before.

Right. Log it. Communication. What you ask for at six in the morning tells him what you think of him. You pointed him at the chain, not at you, and you trusted him with the jet out loud. That's the shape the key rewards. Then he read you the whole order without being asked, which tells you how the handover went.

The test center was in a strip mall off the interstate, between a nail salon and a tax office closed for the season. Graham parked facing the front window, turned the engine off and pulled the milk crate up onto the seat. I'll be right here. He uncapped the red pen. That was all.

Inside it smelled like carpet glue and coffee. The administrator at the desk checked Kit's ID against the confirmation and then against Kit's face, slowly, as if she had all day and meant to use it. Locker six. Everything but you goes in it. Coat, phone, keys, watch.

The coat went in. The 2019 sheet went with it, in the inside pocket, folded around Graham's sticky note. It had been in her toolbox lid for seven years and in that pocket since March, and this was the closest it had been to a test since the one it came from.

Something to write on is on the desk. The clock's in the corner of your screen. If you need me, raise your hand. Eight booths, a man in the corner already typing at something else. Kit sat down in booth three and put both hands flat on the desk, and only then noticed nobody had told her to. In 2019 a man at the front of a room had told them all to. She took her hands off the desk.
Verbal Analogies. Eight minutes. Question three.
Chock is to wheel as anchor is to what?
CHOCK is to WHEEL as ANCHOR is to what?

A chock keeps a wheel from going anywhere. An anchor keeps a ship from going anywhere. She clicked it and was on question four before she noticed she'd liked that one, the whole heavy thing pulling against something that wouldn't let go of it.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Function. A chock holds a wheel still, and an anchor holds a ship still. Chain's a part of it. Harbor's a place. Sailor's the fellow with the sore back. All in the family, and only the ship fits the sentence. That's the habit, Sergeant, on question three of the real one.

She finished Verbal Analogies with forty seconds left and didn't spend them. The screen said Arithmetic Reasoning, twenty nine minutes, and she could hear Vern at his yellow table in February, tapping the egg timer.
It comes right after a fast one. Read the first one twice.
A truck uses eighteen gallons of fuel on a two hundred eighty eight mile trip. At the same rate, how many gallons will it use on a four hundred mile trip?

The first time through, her pencil had already started dividing 400 by something before she knew what she wanted. She put it down and read it again, slower, the way you'd read a fuel slip somebody else had filled out.
Eighteen gallons for 288 miles. At the same rate, how many for 400 miles?
A. Twenty five, at sixteen miles a gallon.
B. Sixteen, the miles it gets on a gallon.
C. Thirty two, twice the sixteen.
D. About twenty two, from 400 times 16 over 288.

She wrote it small. 288 over 18 is 16 miles a gallon. 400 over 16 is 25 gallons. Then the other way, to check: 25 times 16 is 400. Twenty five. It took her less time than the second read had, and Vern would have called that cheap at the price.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Rate first, then the question. 288 miles on 18 gallons is 16 miles a gallon, and 400 miles at 16 a gallon is 25 gallons. Or cross multiply, 18 over 288 equals x over 400. After a fast block your eyes are still going fast, so read the first one twice. Cheapest insurance on the test, and I sold insurance to nobody.

Word Knowledge went by in five minutes like weather through an open hangar door. She knew most of them. One she'd never seen in her life, and she broke it into pieces the way Vern had taught her, guessed from the root, and went on without looking back at it.
Math Knowledge, twenty two minutes. She'd done twenty two minutes of it on Vern's egg timer every week since March, and the clock in the corner of the screen looked like an old friend's.
If five x plus three equals two x minus twelve, then x equals what?
She took the 2x over and the 3 over. Three x on one side. On the other, twelve and three together, fifteen, and in front of the fifteen a minus sign about the size of a lash.

Minus five. She put it back in because Vern would have. Five times minus five is minus twenty five, plus three, minus twenty two. Two times minus five is minus ten, minus twelve, minus twenty two. Same on both sides. She clicked it, and in her head he set his pencil down.

Right. Log it. Subtract 2x from both sides and 3 from both sides: 3x equals minus 15, so x is minus 5. Then plug it in, minus 22 on each side. On Math Knowledge a sign is worth the same as a whole problem, and checking costs ten seconds.

Reading Comprehension was five passages on her form and twenty four minutes, and she kept a finger on the line before she picked, the way she'd learned on a water notice in February. One passage was about a ferry company in the 1800s. She'd have read the rest of it if they'd let her.
Then Situational Judgment. Sixteen, the screen said, in thirty five minutes. She set her halfway mark at eight and seventeen minutes and started.

You're a lieutenant. A senior airman in your section asks for two afternoons a week off the schedule to study for an officer test. Their sergeant tells you the airman is the best mechanic in the section, and the section can't spare them during next month's inspection.
She read it twice, and not because it came after a fast block.
The airman wants study time, and the sergeant needs the airman. What's most effective?
A. Approve the time, and tell the sergeant to find the coverage.
B. Send it to the commander, and let them decide between the two.
C. Sit down with the sergeant first, then plan the coverage together.
D. Tell the airman to wait until the inspection is over.

She clicked it. For least effective she took the one that sent it to the commander, two people who could have settled it at one table and a lieutenant sending it up the building instead. Then she went on to problem six, and it was about a broken printer, and she was grateful.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Resource Management and Mentoring. You go to the person who owns the schedule, privately and first, and you work out a plan that covers the inspection and still grows the airman. The key leans toward finding a way to do both at the lowest level before anything goes up.
At the break she ate the peanut butter crackers Graham had put in her coat pocket and drank a cup of water from the cooler in the lobby, standing at the front window.

His truck was in the third row. He had a lab report flat against the steering wheel and the red pen going. He looked up once, at the window, not knowing if she was there, and lifted the pen an inch off the paper. That was his wave. She didn't go out. She walked the lobby twice and went back to booth three.

Somewhere in the middle of Situational Judgment she'd met herself, the way she'd been in 2019. An airman with a want and a sergeant with an inspection, and nobody ever having to decide anything, because she'd said yes before anybody could ask her what she wanted. Problem five of sixteen, on a screen in Kansas City, and she'd had to read it twice to see it was her.

The inventory came up. Two hundred forty statements, forty five minutes, a row of five marks from strongly disagree to strongly agree. In 2019 she'd done these on paper, the whole stack, as the crew chief she thought a board would want.
I tell people plainly what I want. Strongly disagree, moderately disagree, neither, moderately agree, strongly agree.
She'd have marked this one differently in 2019. What does Kit do with it?
A. Mark Strongly agree, because an officer ought to.
B. Mark what she'd have said in 2019, so she stays consistent.
C. Think about what each mark would say about her, then pick.
D. Mark what's true of her today.

Agree. Not strongly. She was new at it. Next statement. She went through the rest at a walk, the way you'd walk a jet you knew, and didn't look back at one of them. When the clock had six minutes left she was done, and she closed her eyes.

That'll hold, Sergeant. The inventory, taken honestly. First honest mark, quickly, the same way all the way through, about eleven seconds each. Nothing to win. In March I wrote twenty of my own for you at my table, and when you changed number eleven I told you those were yours. These are too.

Physical Science, twenty in ten. The first one was about a lens, and she knew it, and the second about a pulley, and she knew that too, because there'd been a card on the crib rail with four strands drawn on it.
A pickup's tire pressure reads higher after a long highway drive than it did that morning. Why?
She thought of the left main on two two eight in March, worn to limits, and Boyd's rule that you check tire pressure cold or you don't check it at all.
The tire reads higher after a long drive than it did that morning. Why?
A. The tire stretched on the highway, so the air got squeezed.
B. Air that's been moving weighs more, so the gauge reads high.
C. The rubber got hot and shrank down on the air.
D. The air in it got hotter with nowhere to go.

Same tire, same air, hotter. Graham had a card on the rail for that one, a lopsided tire on the front and on the back, SAME SPACE. MORE HEAT. MORE PUSH. She clicked it. In her head Boyd was squatting by the left main in March with his gauge, telling her it'd lie to her for an hour yet.

Right. Log it. Gases, Sergeant. Same space, more heat, more push. Heat air you can't let out. The little fellows in there speed up. They bang the walls more, and the gauge counts every bang. Boyd's rule about checking two two eight's tires cold is that physics with a flight chief's face on it. Don't tell him I said so. You had twenty seconds to spare.
Table Reading went fast and clean. Column, then row, then the cell. Gene's new chart had cured her of trusting where a number used to sit.

Then Instrument Comprehension. Two dials and four little airplanes, twenty five times, in five minutes. In 2019 this was where the paper ran out on her. She'd guessed the last nine, filling in circles with the man at the front of the room counting down, and walked out to her truck and sat there with the engine off.
She took them the way Vern had drawn them on the slate in April. Compass first. Then the bank. Then the pitch. Cross off the moment a cue missed, and go.

Question seventeen was where she'd run out in 2019. She was on it with time on the clock. The horizon line sat below the little airplane, and its left end rode higher than its right. The pointer at the top sat off zero to the left. The compass said west.
Horizon below the little airplane, higher on the left. Compass on west. Which picture?
A. Climbing, banked right, the nose pointed to her left.
B. Climbing, banked left, the nose pointed to her left.
C. Climbing, banked left, the nose pointed to her right.
D. Diving, banked left, the nose pointed to her left.

West, so the nose went to her left. You always stand south of these airplanes looking north, like a man waiting on a bus. Line high on the left and the pointer with it, left wing down. Line under the little airplane, nose up. One picture standing. She clicked it and went on, and when the five minutes ran out she had two left to guess instead of nine.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Compass first. West puts the nose to your left, looking north. Then bank, high end of the line is the low wing, and the pointer backs it up. Then pitch, line under the little airplane, so climbing. Three cues, three cross offs, and you'd quit thinking about 2019 by the second one.

Block Counting, thirty in five. She learned each pile on its first question and counted top, bottom, then around, the same way round every time. On the third pile a block sat up on top of nothing she could see, and she was back at the kitchen table with Graham's cutting board. Something had to be holding it up.
She counted the one she couldn't see and moved on.
Then the last block. Aviation Information, twenty in eight. Her eyes were tired and her back was tired, and she sat up straight anyway, because it was the last eight minutes and they counted.
Ice blocks an airplane's pitot tube, but its static port stays open. Which instrument stops reading correctly?
Ice over the pitot tube, and the static port is clear. What stops reading right?
Airspeed. Both holes. She clicked it. Forty seconds, two open. C and A, on purpose. Then the screen thanked her like a vending machine, and that was all five hours.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Pitot and static. Airspeed is a fellow comparing two breaths, the ram air in the pitot tube and the still air at the static port. Plug the pitot and he's comparing one breath to nothing. Altimeter and vertical speed live off the static port alone. That pair was in April's lesson, and it showed up on question eighteen of the last block.

At five to one on Saturday she came out into the parking lot with her coat over her arm. Graham was standing by the truck. The milk crate was on the hood with ninety six lab reports in it, graded, squared at the corners. He didn't ask. She got in, and he got in, and at the first stoplight she said she hadn't run out on the dials. He reached over and put his hand on the back of her neck until the light changed.
Her phone had come out of the locker with a text on it from Fisk, sent at 7:41 that morning.
A text from Fisk. She's off. On time.
On Monday Boyd texted that number three was getting a new fuel control, the leak check run was Tuesday at six in the evening, and she was on it. Nothing else.

On Tuesday she worked the eleven to seven at the plant. At ten after six in the morning, at the break table, with the flow meter ticking over at 1.3 and Gene not in yet, she tried the score page on her phone again, the way she had on Monday.
The score lookup page. Social, last name, test center number. She typed them in a second time to be sure.
She hit enter with her thumb shaking a little, which she'd have denied.
The score report. Six composites down the page, and Situational Judgment on its own line under them.
She read the top line twice. Situational Judgment, on its own line at the bottom, was the best number on the page, and she'd have to think later about what that meant.
It's ten after six, and the number's on her phone. Who does Kit call first?
A. Graham, at the house, before he's out the door for first period.
B. Colonel Merritt's office, to bring her the number as promised.
C. The shop's group text, so all of them hear it at once.
D. Vern, who's been up for an hour, and who taught her every Tuesday.

He picked up on the first ring. Coffee maker, radio on low. He was by the sink. She could tell. Eighty one. He didn't say anything for a while. Then she heard him set his mug down on the counter, carefully, the way you'd set down something you didn't want to spill. I'll see you after. He meant after her run tonight. It was only a word, for once.

Right. Log it. Communication. The person it touches most hears it first, from you, in your own voice. He drove you, he waited five hours in a parking lot, and he'd waited a lot longer than that for an after that wasn't a wait. When news touches several people, the ones it affects most hear it directly and early, before anybody else.

Corbin heard it next, the way she'd told him in March. He picked up on the first ring, the way he'd said he would, and when she told him he was quiet long enough that she heard the shop radio behind him. Then he said he'd be at the far bench all week if she wanted to hear about the first week of anything.

Rhonda picked up on the second ring and cried from hello to goodbye. Don't you ask me what hurts, Kitty. Nothing hurts. Then, blowing her nose, Can I tell Darlene? She's the one who told me the last thing. Kit said she could tell Darlene.
At noon she called Cedar Street and told Vern, and said she'd miss seven o'clock tonight, and why. He said north fence, then.

At two she put the printout on Boyd's desk. He read it, set it down, and picked it up again. Hundred forty four with the CSO. Page two wanted fifty. He'd added it before she could. Run's at six. Number three. You're on it. He'd put her on it Monday, a day before there was any number to have. He'd picked the day.

At three she climbed the stairs in the wing headquarters building and waited on the landing until it was three exactly. She'd told Merritt she'd bring the number, so she brought it. Merritt read it with one finger on the top line. I'll write the endorsement tonight. I asked Haas at noon if I could put him in it. He said tell them. She squared the printout to the edge of the desk. So they'll read about him first. Then you.

From the truck she called the base test office and booked the TBAS, Thursday, June 10, at nine. She texted Graham the date. The board was July 10, and she didn't say anything to herself about the board.
A text from Graham. Board's got a new column.

He'd sent a picture. Past Sunday, May 9, the last square he'd drawn in February, past the aluminum edge, he'd taped a strip of paper to the fridge and drawn a new column in his black. JUNE 10, TBAS. JULY 10, BOARD. At the top of it, for this Saturday, small: STAIN.
She sat in the truck in the headquarters lot and looked at STAIN until the phone went dark, and then she woke it up and looked again. She wrote back with one thumb.
A text from Kit. Saturday. I'll find the brushes.

At half past five, at her toolbox, she took the 2019 sheet out of her coat and unfolded it on the lid. Pilot 19, and under it, in Vern's capitals, ACUITY. She wrote the new number under his word, in pencil, the first thing she'd ever written on it.
Out the shop window Vern and Patrice were at the north fence, outside it, where the county road ran along the ramp. Patrice had brought a folding chair and was not using it.
His word's on her sheet, and her number's under it now. What does Kit do with it?
A. Pin it on the shop corkboard by the coffee, where the posting went up.
B. Put it back under the foam in her toolbox lid, where it lived for years.
C. Drop it in the shop's burn bin and be done with 2019.
D. Take it out to the fence and ask Vern if his word can stay.

She walked it out to the fence, folded it small and pushed it through one of the diamonds in the chain link. Your word's on my sheet, sir. Can it stay there? He unfolded it against the fence post and read it with his glasses down, the old number, his word, her pencil under it. He read it a long time. That's more than one line, Sergeant. He took his time folding it back up on her creases. Then he poked it through the wire at her. Keep it. I know how it's spelled.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Communication, the last time I'll say it. Somebody else's mark on your page? Ask them first. Directly and privately, and then you let them answer. Through a chain link fence, no less, and Patrice watching. I've had my copy of that word since 1973.
Patrice had come up beside him, small in a gray cardigan, with her reading glasses pushed up into her hair.
Vern reached into his shirt pocket, behind the pencil and the envelope, and handed her a log through the chain link, folded small.
Fourteen December, oh one. Two two eight. My last one at the table. Gave the Lieutenant the last fix. She had it already. Told her anyway.
Is that the last one in the box? It's the last one I wrote. You still don't get the box.

Patrice looked past both of them at the jet. The power cart was running, and Fisk was out by the nose with the headset cord over his shoulder. I was down the hall. He told you I have a word for it. I don't need one. I knew the first year, and I let him have the seat. Vern didn't say anything. He put his hand on the fence, his fingers through the wire, and the ring on it was the one in her mother's picture.

Kit walked back across the ramp. Boyd's truck sat off the left wingtip, where he could see the window with her name under it, with the windows down and the engine off. He didn't get out. He lifted two fingers off the wheel, the way he had at her first engine run in 2018, and he hadn't gotten out for that one either.
At ten after six on a Tuesday evening in May, Kit Darrow sat in the left seat of a jet that wasn't allowed to go anywhere.

Two two eight was chocked front and back, brake set, throttles up at run power, and every rivet in her was shoving at chocks that weren't going anywhere either. Out front the north ramp was dry, and past the hangars was the Missouri, which at that hour you could actually see. Seventy one degrees outside. Somebody had left a Dr Pepper can on the glare shield, and she moved it. Night shift had changed the fuel control on number three, and this was the leak check.
Three's dry, Sergeant. No leaks. I looked twice.

She checked three's gauges against the other three engines, all of them about where they ought to be, and wrote the numbers on her card in her own bad printing. Then she held them there a second longer than she needed to. Behind her were the bolt holes where the nav seat had been bolted down in 1962. She didn't have to turn around for those. Up top was Vern's little round cap, painted over twice since 2001. She had the interphone switched off, and at run power Fisk couldn't have heard her if he'd been sitting in her lap. She said it out loud anyway.
Then she keyed the interphone. Copy. Bringing them back.

She pulled the throttles back, and the jet settled onto its gear. She ran the shutdown checklist. After the last engine quit she stayed put, listening to the gyros wind down and the metal tick. Out the windscreen Fisk was coiling the headset cord, hand over hand, the way she'd taught him, and past him, at the fence, somebody small in a gray cardigan was waving with both arms. Beside her, Vern had one hand up, pointing at the sky.
